title: What Changed This Month: From Chat to Custom Interfaces and Smarter Agent Workflows
question: What changed this month, and which developments matter most to a learning programmer?
argument: This month, the shift from chat-based AI interfaces to customizable, interactive canvases and the integration of smarter agent workflows fundamentally changes how learners can delegate programming tasks and interact with coding agents.
synthesis: Combining GitHub's introduction of canvases as customizable UIs for AI interaction with OpenAI's Computer Use agents that operate full Linux virtual computers shows a move beyond simple chat prompts to richer, more autonomous agent workflows. Simon Willison's voice-driven coding demo illustrates practical multitasking with agents, while GitHub's guidance on teaching Copilot about codebases highlights how learners can tailor agent behavior to their projects. Together, these developments enable learners to delegate more complex tasks safely and interactively, improving productivity and control.
limitations: Most evidence comes from vendor blogs and demos, which may emphasize potential over widespread adoption. Independent studies on learner outcomes with these new interfaces are lacking. The complexity of setting up custom canvases or agents might be a barrier for beginners. The podcast and blog examples focus on experienced developers or creators, not novices.

claims.statement: GitHub introduced canvases in the Copilot app, customizable full-stack interfaces that allow bidirectional interaction between the user and AI agents, enabling richer workflows beyond chat.

locator.quote: There are lots of ways to pull this off, but in the GitHub Copilot app, this is called a canvas.

A canvas is a little full-stack application that runs inside of the GitHub Copilot app with no browser chrome. The agent can communicate with the server part of that app and the server can communicate back. So what you end up with is a surface that can do anything a normal computer program can do, plus can communicate bi-directionally with the GitHub Copilot agent.

That sounds very hand-wavy and I did use the word bi-directional which sounds like it’s straight off of a PowerPoint, so let’s look at this concept in practice and see if we can solve actual problems with the mighty canvas.
Here’s a full example of how you can use a canvas to automate your own workflow, removing yourself from the loop as much or as little as you like.

claims.statement: GitHub Copilot app now supports custom instructions, agent skills, custom agents, and MCP servers to tailor AI behavior to specific codebases and workflows, improving agent usefulness and context awareness.

locator.quote: Context matters when you’re working with AI. Every codebase has its own house rules: how components are structured, which scripts to run, and which conventions apply to different frameworks and file types.
Custom instructions communicate the conventions Copilot should follow.
Package repeatable procedures as agent skills

Custom agents let you create specialized versions of Copilot for work like this. A repository-level agent profile lives in .github/agents and can define the agent’s purpose, instructions, tools, and relevant project context.
Instructions, skills, and agents help Copilot understand how to work within your project. MCP servers expand what it can access and do beyond the repository.

claims.statement: OpenAI's Computer Use agents run on personal Linux virtual computers in the cloud, allowing them to perform complex tasks autonomously, such as meal ordering, saving users significant time.
Simon Willison demonstrated building a new blog feature almost entirely by voice using Codex in a local development environment, showing practical voice-driven coding workflows.

locator.quote: I shipped a new feature for my blog today: the Newsletters page, which offers an index of all of the newsletters I’ve sent out, both my free weekly Substack and my monthly sponsors-only updates. I built the feature almost entirely using my voice, chatting away to my laptop while I cooked dinner.
We went on like this for about half an hour (the time it took to cook dinner). The model would reply and occasionally ask clarifying questions, then get to work modifying the code.

claims.statement: Learners can now delegate more complex, multi-step tasks to AI agents using these new interfaces and workflows, reducing manual implementation time while retaining control through review and guidance.

locator.quote: But here’s the thing. I don’t actually need to be around for most of this process. The agent is capable of researching and generating prototypes and then letting me know when it’s ready for a review. The goal with agents is always to take yourself out of the loop as much as you can. That’s difficult though, because it’s not clear how to do that when all you have is a chat box.

Notice what changed. You’re still responsible for the outcome, but you’re spending less time implementing every piece yourself. Instead, you’re defining the work, reviewing outputs, and making the technical decisions that bring everything together.

title: Scrutinizing Claims About Coding Agents: Trust, Reliability, and Intervention
question: Which claims about coding agents withstand scrutiny, and where are evidence or interpretations in tension?
argument: Claims about coding agents' reliability and trustworthiness reveal persistent challenges: agents often fail silently, necessitating human intervention and review, and while new tools improve intervention timing and code review, learners must remain vigilant.
synthesis: Stack Overflow's analysis of silent failures and trust erosion in AI tools highlights a fundamental reliability problem, supported by arXiv research on intervention sentinels that improve task completion by pre-execution checks. GitHub's ReviewBench benchmark provides a rigorous framework to evaluate AI code reviewers, confirming that agent outputs vary in quality and require human judgment. Together, these sources show that despite advances, learners cannot fully trust agents to produce correct code without review and must learn when and how to intervene effectively.
limitations: The Stack Overflow article relies on surveys and anecdotal evidence from 2024-2025, which may not fully reflect current model capabilities. The arXiv intervention sentinel research is experimental and may not yet be integrated into mainstream tools. GitHub's ReviewBench is vendor-provided and may reflect internal priorities. There is limited direct evidence on novice learners' ability to judge agent output quality.

claims.statement: AI coding agents can produce silent failures where tasks appear to complete successfully but no meaningful work is done, undermining trust.

locator.quote: Every trust instrument a developer owns—exit codes, green CI, a passing status check, the words "task complete"—rests on an assumption that software fails loudly. Unattended agents fail quietly. A loop can terminate cleanly, report success, and have produced nothing at all, and there is no signal anywhere in your stack that distinguishes that from a job well done. Call it the silent green exit.

When an agent loop exits 0, the integer is emitted by an orchestrator that stopped looping because the model produced a token meaning "done." Nothing between the model's claim and the exit code checked anything. The status is a self-assessment, and you have plugged it into a socket built for an observation. Every consumer downstream—your dashboard, your alerting rules, your retry logic, the person who glances at a run history on Monday morning—inherits that substitution without ever being told it happened.

"Almost right, but not quite" describes an output you can look at. What I'm describing sits one level beneath it: a run that isn't almost right but empty, and that presents identically to a run that worked.

claims.statement: Developer trust in AI tools has declined as usage increased, with many frustrated by outputs that are almost right but not quite, highlighting reliability issues.

locator.quote: Donovan cites this site's own Developer Survey on the trust divergence, and it's worth pulling the primary figures because the shape is stark. Between the 2024 and 2025 surveys, the share of developers using or planning to use AI tools rose from 76% to 84%, while the share who trust the accuracy of what those tools produce fell from 43% to 33%. Active distrust went the other way, from 30% to 46%. The single biggest frustration, cited by 66%, was "AI solutions that are almost right, but not quite."

claims.statement: HiSentinel, a hindsight-distilled sentinel model, can preemptively decide when to intervene in coding agent actions to improve task completion and reduce error propagation.

locator.quote: Abstract:Coding agents solve repository-level tasks through sequences of actions, where a single erroneous action can misdirect subsequent decisions and increase recovery costs. Existing approaches use execution feedback for recovery or specialized checks to block errors, but deciding before execution whether intervention will benefit eventual task completion remains challenging. To address this challenge, we propose HiSentinel, a hindsight-distillation framework that trains lightweight 0.6B and 1.7B sentinels to select pre-execution interventions aimed at improving task completion rather than correcting every imperfect action. A privileged teacher uses recorded execution outcomes as evidenc

e for intervention judgments, which are distilled into a causal student that receives only the pre-action context and proposed action. Beyond identifying whether and when to intervene, the sentinel must also provide actionable feedback that helps the coding agent recover or obtain necessary human input. To support these capabilities, we introduce SWE-Intervene, an action-level dataset constructed from software-engineering trajectories that annotates whether an action should be allowed, autonomously redirected, or paused for human assistance, together with corresponding intervention feedback. Across SWE-bench Verified Mini and Ask or Assume, HiSentinel consistently improves task completion ac

ross Sentinel scales and coding-agent families, with gains of up to 14% and 10%, respectively, while maintaining competitive token consumption. These results demonstrate that lightweight pre-execution intervention can effectively prevent error propagation and improve the reliability of autonomous coding agents.

claims.statement: ReviewBench is a new comprehensive benchmark for AI code review agents that measures their ability to catch issues with calibrated evaluation and correlates well with production performance.

locator.quote: Agentic code review is becoming an essential piece of how development happens. It helps you inspect pull requests, catch issues, and decide what deserves attention before code ships.

We built ReviewBench, a new code review offline benchmark, to address that gap, and it is available for you to use today. It follows the language, repo size, and size distribution of pull requests, modeled after over 100 million real pull requests on GitHub. It uses a multi-source golden set and a consistent evaluation rubric and has been independently validated by senior engineers. Just as important, with the help of ReviewBench, our offline evaluation of Copilot code review (CCR) has become more effective at anticipating the direction of production experiments, giving us greater confidence that measured improvements reflect meaningful gains for users.
219 public pull requests across 19 languages, aligned to GitHub-wide distributions while preserving substantive review cases.

claims.statement: Learners must maintain human oversight and develop skills to evaluate and intervene in AI-generated code, as agents alone cannot guarantee correctness or completeness.

locator.quote: I built ProAI, one of the first commercialized GPT products, and I now work on multi-agent systems and how to evaluate them before they go anywhere near production; I write about that at chasewhughes.com. This is the failure mode I think we are least prepared for, and it gets a fraction of the coverage that capability and safety do, because reliability is the least interesting of the three to write about and the only one that decides whether you can use the thing.

ross Sentinel scales and coding-agent families, with gains of up to 14% and 10%, respectively, while maintaining competitive token consumption. These results demonstrate that lightweight pre-execution intervention can effectively prevent error propagation and improve the reliability of autonomous coding agents.

But the quality of existing AI reviewers can be hard to measure, and you need to know the strengths of a reviewer before you know if it will help you. Some reviewers surface more issues, some produce less noise, and some are stronger at catching critical problems while others surface smaller improvements, too. You may need code review to do different things within your workflow.

title: Implications for Learners: How to Work, Study, and What to Watch Next
question: What do these developments imply for how a learner should work and study, and what should they watch next?
argument: Learners should adopt interactive, context-aware AI workflows, strengthen their skills in directing and reviewing AI outputs, and watch for tools that improve agent reliability and intervention to safely delegate more programming tasks.
synthesis: GitHub's advice to learn to direct AI and evaluate its output, combined with the practical voice-driven coding example from Simon Willison and the customizable canvases for workflow automation, suggests learners should actively shape agent behavior and maintain review habits. The latent-space podcast's insights on Computer Use agents show the potential for significant time savings when delegating complex tasks. Meanwhile, the arXiv research on spec-driven lifecycles and intervention sentinels points to emerging best practices for integrating agents safely. Learners should watch for advances in agent autonomy balanced with intervention tools and benchmarks like ReviewBench to guide trust.
limitations: Most guidance comes from vendor sources and early research; independent studies on learning outcomes are scarce. The complexity of new tools may overwhelm beginners without instructor support. Rapidly evolving agent capabilities mean learners must stay updated continuously.

claims.statement: Learners should focus on learning to direct AI agents effectively, providing clear context and evaluating multiple AI outputs critically before accepting code.

locator.quote: Tip #1: Learn to direct AI, not just use it.
AI can generate impressive solutions in seconds, but the first answer isn’t always the best. Your experience writing clean, maintainable code can help you evaluate AI’s output.
Ask a second AI model to critique the first model’s work, then use your own judgment to evaluate both responses.

claims.statement: Using customizable canvases and custom instructions allows learners to tailor AI behavior to their projects, improving productivity and reducing repetitive explanations.

locator.quote: Repository custom instructions give Copilot that baseline context. Add a .github/copilot-instructions.md file to define guidance that applies across the repository, such as your preferred architecture, naming conventions, or expectations for testing and validation.
To create a canvas, you don’t have to do any coding or design by hand. Just open an agent session, enter the /create-canvas skill, and describe what you want in plain English.

Not sure where to begin? The community has shared ready-made canvas extensions through Awesome Copilot, including release notes tools, kanban boards, issue triage workflows, and more. Install one that’s close to what you need, then ask the agent to customize it for your workflow in the same way you would refine a canvas you created yourself.

As AI takes on more implementation work, the skills that distinguish great engineers become even more important: exercising sound judgment, balancing tradeoffs, and solving the right problems.

Learners should start small by adding one project convention as a custom instruction to Copilot and gradually build up more tailored AI workflows.

locator.quote: Start small: choose one convention you keep explaining, add it to .github/copilot-instructions.md, and see how Copilot applies it to your next task.
